screens.title: Why advanced client interactions matter
screens.narratorSegment: A polished DApp treats the user experience as primary because blockchain operations are asynchronous and sometimes slow. Advanced client interactions are the techniques that bridge on-chain state and the user's expectations. Concretely, this means pushing updates from the network into your UI instead of waiting for the user to refresh, giving clear progress and confirmation messages during transactions, and mapping raw errors into actionable help. For example, when a counter program increases a value, a subscription can push that new value to your app immediately so the user sees the change without reloading. A common misconception is that polling is sufficient; while polling works for small demos, it wastes resources and can miss rapid changes. Another pitfall is showing raw blockchain errors; users see cryptic text and abandon the app. The practical significance is trust: immediate and accurate feedback reduces confusion, prevents users from resending transactions, and avoids unnecessary fees. As you apply these ideas, ask yourself which user action currently feels uncertain in your app and choose one interaction to make deterministic and visible. Why advanced client interactions matter means timely state updates and friendly errors make blockchain apps usable and avoid wasted actions.. In practical terms, turning asynchronous blockchain events into clear user feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why advanced client interactions matter

Advanced client interactions convert asynchronous blockchain events into clear, predictable UI behavior. They include real-time updates, confirmation flows, and user-friendly error handling.

Definition: Client interactions are how your app communicates state changes and outcomes to a user when on-chain events occur.
Example: A counter increment triggers an onAccountChange update that sets React state to the new count.
Misconception: Polling at slow intervals is enough. It often leads to stale UIs and poor UX.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize push updates and clear confirmations to keep users informed and avoid unnecessary transactions.

Concrete scenario

Your user presses "Increment Counter". Without a subscription the UI waits for a manual refresh; with a subscription the UI updates when the account changes. With proper confirmation the app will show pending, then confirmed, avoiding duplicate clicks.

Try this: identify one button in your DApp that currently leaves the user guessing, and plan a subscription or a confirmation step to make it obvious.
Common mistake: showing network errors verbatim. Always translate errors into actions the user can take.

screens.title: WebSocket subscriptions on Solana
screens.narratorSegment: WebSocket subscriptions let the Solana RPC node push updates to your client when a monitored account changes. This is different from polling because the node sends messages only when data changes, which is efficient and timely. The core A P I shown here is connection. onAccountChange(accountPublicKey, callback, commitment). The callback receives an accountInfo object containing the latest account data, which you should deserialize using your program's coder. A concrete example is subscribing to a counter PDA; when the program updates the counter, the RPC notifies every subscribed client and your callback deserializes and updates React state. A common misconception is that subscription callbacks replace all fetching; they complement an initial fetch. Always perform an initial fetch to populate state, then rely on the subscription to keep it fresh. Finally, remember that subscriptions have lifetimes tied to your connection and component lifecycle; failing to remove listeners on unmount can leak memory and produce stale updates. The practical takeaway is simple: subscriptions keep UI state current and reduce unnecessary load while improving user experience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Definition

WebSocket subscriptions

Subscriptions allow the RPC to push messages to your client when specific accounts or logs change. They are more efficient and immediate than periodic polling.

API: connection.onAccountChange(publicKey, callback, commitment)
Example: subscribe to a counter PDA and update state when the account changes.
Misconception: subscriptions alone are enough. Always fetch initial state before relying on updates.
Subscription flow
  1. Initial fetch: program.account.counter.fetch(pda) to populate UI.
  2. Set up listener: connection.onAccountChange(pda, callback, 'confirmed').
  3. Deserialize: use program.coder.accounts.decode to read account data.
  4. Cleanup: connection.removeAccountChangeListener(id) on unmount.
Key Takeaway

Subscriptions provide timely updates. Use an initial fetch, then subscribe, and always remove the listener on cleanup.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the practical useEffect pattern that subscribes to a counter PDA and updates state on changes. The approach combines an initial fetch with a subscription so the UI is always accurate. First, derive the PDA for the user's counter and perform an initial program. account. counter. fetch to set the counter value. Second, call connection. onAccountChange with the PDA and a callback that deserializes accountInfo. data using program. coder. accounts. decode, then call setCounterValue. Third, store the listener id and return a cleanup function that calls connection. removeAccountChangeListener(id). A concrete example is provided in the chapter and shows handling decode errors inside the callback; log and ignore decode problems so a transient update does not crash the UI. A common error is forgetting to guard for missing program or connection, producing runtime exceptions. Also avoid calling setState on an unmounted component by removing the listener in the cleanup. This pattern ensures the user sees immediate updates after any state change on-chain, and it prevents memory leaks or duplicated listeners when dependencies change. keyIdea.title: Fetch, subscribe, cleanup
keyIdea.text: Combine initial fetch with onAccountChange and remove the listener on unmount.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

useEffect subscription pattern

This code shows initial fetch, subscription callback, and cleanup in a React useEffect for FullCounterDApp.

// Inside FullCounterDApp.tsx useEffect
useEffect(() => {
  if (!wallet || !connection) {
    setCounterValue(null);
    setCounterAccountPublicKey(null);
    return;
  }

  const program = getProgram();
  if (!program) return;

  let listenerId = null;

  const setup = async () => {
    try {
      const [pda] = PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync(
        [Buffer.from("counter"), wallet.publicKey.toBuffer()],
        PROGRAM_ID
      );
      setCounterAccountPublicKey(pda);

      const counterAccount = await program.account.counter.fetch(pda);
      setCounterValue(counterAccount.count.toNumber());

      listenerId = connection.onAccountChange(
        pda,
        (accountInfo) => {
          try {
            const deserialized = program.coder.accounts.decode("Counter", accountInfo.data);
            setCounterValue(deserialized.count.toNumber());
          } catch (err) {
            console.error("Decode error:", err);
          }
        },
        'confirmed'
      );
    } catch (e) {
      console.error(e);
      setCounterValue(0);
    }
  };

  setup();

  return () => {
    if (listenerId !== null) connection.removeAccountChangeListener(listenerId);
  };
}, [wallet, connection, getProgram]);
Explanation
  • Guard for wallet and connection to avoid errors.
  • Perform an initial fetch to populate state before subscribing.
  • Deserialize accountInfo.data with program.coder.accounts.decode.
  • Always remove the listener on cleanup to prevent leaks.
Pro tip: log decode errors but avoid showing them to users; instead show a friendly fallback.
Key Takeaway

Use a combined fetch + subscription pattern and ensure cleanup to keep UI accurate and memory safe.

screens.title: Cleaning up listeners and avoiding memory leaks
screens.narratorSegment: Cleaning up listeners is essential to avoid memory leaks, duplicate callbacks, and confusing UI updates. When a component mounts it may add an onAccountChange listener; if the component unmounts or dependencies change without removing that listener, callbacks can continue to run and attempt to update state for an unmounted component. The process is straightforward: store the listener id returned by connection. onAccountChange, and in the useEffect cleanup call connection. removeAccountChangeListener(id) if id is not null. An example flow: start loading, compute PDA, fetch initial data, set up listener and save its id, and finally return a cleanup closure that removes the listener. A common misconception is that React will automatically remove external subscriptions; it won't. Another pitfall is not handling async setup order, which can cause the cleanup to have no id. To avoid this, declare the listener id in the outer scope of the effect and set it inside the async setup function. The practical benefit is predictable behavior: when the user navigates away or switches wallets, your app stops listening, preventing stale updates and console noise. Cleaning up listeners and avoiding memory leaks means store listener ids and remove them in the cleanup to prevent background callbacks and leaks.. In practical terms, why and how to remove account change listeners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Always remove listeners
keyIdea.text: Store listener IDs and remove them in the cleanup to prevent background callbacks and leaks.

content.html:
Process Flow

Listener lifecycle

  1. Declare listenerId in the effect scope as null.
  2. After creating the subscription, assign the returned id to listenerId.
  3. Return a cleanup function that checks listenerId and calls removeAccountChangeListener.
  4. Also handle connection or wallet changes by re-running effect and cleaning previous listener.
Common mistake: assigning listener id inside an inner scope and returning a cleanup that sees null. Keep id in the outer closure.
Concrete example

Declare let listenerId = null at the top of the effect, set listenerId = connection.onAccountChange(...), and in return() call connection.removeAccountChangeListener(listenerId) if it exists.

Why it matters: prevents duplicate logs, prevents callbacks trying to update unmounted components, and reduces server-side subscription load.
Check: when switching wallets, ensure old listeners are removed before establishing new ones.
Key Takeaway

Manage listener IDs explicitly and always remove them on cleanup to keep behavior predictable and efficient.

screens.title: Transaction confirmation and user feedback
screens.narratorSegment: Transactions on Solana go through stages: you send a transaction and receive a signature, validators process it, and the network reaches a chosen confirmation level such as confirmed or finalized. For a great UX, your app should surface these stages to the user. After sending a transaction and receiving its signature, call connection. getLatestBlockhash to obtain the recent blockhash and then connection. confirmTransaction with the blockhash, lastValidBlockHeight, and signature to wait for confirmation. While waiting, display a pending state or spinner to show progress. Also consider optimistic UI: update non-critical UI elements immediately but revert if confirmation fails. A frequent misconception is trusting rpc() alone for finality; rpc may return quickly but not reflect final block inclusion. Another pitfall is not handling timeouts or network errors, which leaves the user waiting indefinitely. Always provide clear next steps: display the signature for advanced users, show a friendly message when confirmation fails, and offer retries or guidance on checking network status. This pattern reduces uncertainty and prevents repeated clicks that could send duplicate transactions. Transaction confirmation and user feedback means await confirmation with the latest blockhash and present pending/confirmed states to users.. In practical terms, how to await finality and show meaningful progress. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Transaction confirmation

Awaiting confirmation ensures the transaction is included in a block and reaches the chosen finality. Use the latest blockhash and confirmTransaction to avoid race conditions.

// Confirmation sequence (conceptual)
const txSignature = await program.methods.increment().rpc();
const latestBlockHash = await connection.getLatestBlockhash();
await connection.confirmTransaction({
  blockhash: latestBlockHash.blockhash,
  lastValidBlockHeight: latestBlockHash.lastValidBlockHeight,
  signature: txSignature,
});
// Update UI after confirmation
User feedback patterns
  • Show pending spinner and disable related buttons.
  • Display concise success notification on confirmation.
  • If failure occurs, show a friendly message and suggested fixes.
Misconception: returning a signature means success. Always confirm using the latest blockhash to ensure inclusion.
Key Takeaway

Present explicit pending and confirmed states, and use confirmTransaction to avoid showing premature success.

screens.title: Error handling patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Error handling in DApps requires anticipating several categories of failure and translating them into messages that help users take the next step. The chapter lists common error categories: wallet connection errors, transaction simulation failures, program runtime errors, and network errors. For example, if a wallet rejects a transaction, show 'Transaction rejected by wallet. Please approve the transaction to continue.' For simulation errors like insufficient funds, suggest checking the SOL balance. For program errors, avoid exposing entire error stacks; parse known custom program error tokens if available and present the mapped cause. For network errors, suggest checking the internet connection or trying again later. A common mistake is displaying raw blockchain errors; these are technical and intimidating. Another pitfall is ignoring retries for transient network issues. content.html:
Code Walkthrough

handleIncrement pattern

const handleIncrement = async () => {
  setIsLoading(true);
  try {
    const txSignature = await program.methods.increment().accounts({ ... }).rpc();
    // Notify user transaction was sent
    const latestBlockHash = await connection.getLatestBlockhash();
    await connection.confirmTransaction({
      blockhash: latestBlockHash.blockhash,
      lastValidBlockHeight: latestBlockHash.lastValidBlockHeight,
      signature: txSignature,
    });
    // Notify user confirmed and refresh
    await fetchCounter();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Transaction failed:", error);
    if (error.message.includes("User rejected the request")) {
      alert("Transaction rejected by wallet.");
    } else if (error.message.includes("custom program error")) {
      alert(`Program error: ${error.message.split("custom program error: ")[1].split(" (")[0]}`);
    } else {
      alert(`Transaction failed: ${error.message || "Unknown error"}`);
    }
  } finally {
    setIsLoading(false);
  }
};
Explanation
  • Set isLoading and disable actions during the flow.
  • Send transaction, then explicitly confirm using the latest blockhash.
  • Catch known errors and present friendly, actionable messages.
Misconception: showing only the signature is sufficient. Instead, show progress and final confirmation to avoid user uncertainty.
Key Takeaway

Translate internal errors into short, helpful messages and keep users informed during confirmation.

content.html:
Architecture

Wallet adapter wrapper pattern

Wrap your app with provider components so your DApp consumes a uniform wallet API regardless of the underlying adapter.

function App() {
  const network = WalletAdapterNetwork.Devnet;
  const endpoint = useMemo(() => clusterApiUrl(network), [network]);
  const wallets = useMemo(() => [new PhantomWalletAdapter(), new SolflareWalletAdapter({ network })], [network]);

  return (
    <ConnectionProvider endpoint={endpoint}>
      <WalletProvider wallets={wallets} autoConnect>
        <WalletModalProvider>
          <WalletMultiButton />
          <FullCounterDApp />
        </WalletModalProvider>
      </WalletProvider>
    </ConnectionProvider>
  );
}
Practical notes
  • Include adapter UI styles as required by the package.
  • Test autoConnect behavior and wallet switching flows.
  • Show truncated public key and connected wallet brand to reassure users.
Misconception: wallet adapters remove the need for error handling. They help with connection flows but you still need to handle rejection and network errors gracefully.
Key Takeaway

Adapters give you consistency. Wrap providers once and use hooks like useWallet across your components.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on making your Solana DApp feel immediate and trustworthy. You will learn how to receive real-time on-chain updates with WebSocket subscriptions, manage transaction confirmation and diverse error states in a way that informs the user, and integrate wallet adapters so connection and signing feel consistent across vendors. I will show concrete examples for subscribing to account changes, using connection. onAccountChange, and improving your handleIncrement flow with clear loading states and friendly error messages. We'll also cover practical UI patterns: clear calls to action, loading and disabled states, and input validation to avoid unnecessary fees. Understanding these patterns matters because blockchain latency and cryptic errors are common causes of user frustration; a well-designed client interaction reduces confusion and increases trust. As you move through the lesson, notice the small code changes that produce smoother feedback and fewer manual refreshes. At the end, reflect on one UX improvement you can apply immediately to your DApp.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to set up real-time updates in a DApp using WebSocket subscriptions so your UI always reflects the latest on-chain data. You will also learn to handle transaction confirmation and multiple error states in a way that provides clear, actionable feedback to users, reducing confusion and support requests. Additionally, you'll design and apply UI patterns that make wallet connections and transaction flows intuitive, including loading states and disabled actions when appropriate. Finally, you'll integrate wallet adapters so your DApp supports multiple wallets consistently without custom per-wallet code. Each objective includes a concrete example: subscribing to a counter account to receive live increments, wrapping transaction sends with confirmation and friendly messages, adding disabled states during sends, and wrapping your app with ConnectionProvider and WalletProvider to use WalletMultiButton. These skills matter because blockchain UX problems often stem from stale data and cryptic errors; mastering these objectives will let you keep users informed, prevent unnecessary fees, and foster trust. Consider which objective you will apply first in your project.

This second objectives slide reinforces what you will practice: building a live counter using onAccountChange, handling confirmation after sending a transaction, and presenting friendly errors for wallet rejections and program failures. You'll learn to integrate wallet adapters and the WalletMultiButton so users can connect without copying keys or switching networks manually. Practically, you will modify FullCounterDApp: set up a useEffect that subscribes to the counter PDA, deserialize account data using the program coder, and update state in the subscription callback. You will also improve handleIncrement to show a loading state, call confirmTransaction with the latest blockhash, and catch specific error messages to present actionable guidance. These tasks matter because they convert asynchronous blockchain events into clear UI responses users can trust. As you complete these steps, note one place in your app where a subscription or improved error message would reduce confusion most immediately.

A polished DApp treats the user experience as primary because blockchain operations are asynchronous and sometimes slow. Advanced client interactions are the techniques that bridge on-chain state and the user's expectations. Concretely, this means pushing updates from the network into your UI instead of waiting for the user to refresh, giving clear progress and confirmation messages during transactions, and mapping raw errors into actionable help. For example, when a counter program increases a value, a subscription can push that new value to your app immediately so the user sees the change without reloading. A common misconception is that polling is sufficient; while polling works for small demos, it wastes resources and can miss rapid changes. Another pitfall is showing raw blockchain errors; users see cryptic text and abandon the app. The practical significance is trust: immediate and accurate feedback reduces confusion, prevents users from resending transactions, and avoids unnecessary fees. As you apply these ideas, ask yourself which user action currently feels uncertain in your app and choose one interaction to make deterministic and visible. Why advanced client interactions matter means timely state updates and friendly errors make blockchain apps usable and avoid wasted actions.. In practical terms, turning asynchronous blockchain events into clear user feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

WebSocket subscriptions let the Solana RPC node push updates to your client when a monitored account changes. This is different from polling because the node sends messages only when data changes, which is efficient and timely. The core A P I shown here is connection. onAccountChange(accountPublicKey, callback, commitment). The callback receives an accountInfo object containing the latest account data, which you should deserialize using your program's coder. A concrete example is subscribing to a counter PDA; when the program updates the counter, the RPC notifies every subscribed client and your callback deserializes and updates React state. A common misconception is that subscription callbacks replace all fetching; they complement an initial fetch. Always perform an initial fetch to populate state, then rely on the subscription to keep it fresh. Finally, remember that subscriptions have lifetimes tied to your connection and component lifecycle; failing to remove listeners on unmount can leak memory and produce stale updates. The practical takeaway is simple: subscriptions keep UI state current and reduce unnecessary load while improving user experience. WebSocket subscriptions on Solana means use onaccountchange to receive account updates and refresh ui state efficiently.. In practical terms, how the cluster pushes account changes to your client. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the practical useEffect pattern that subscribes to a counter PDA and updates state on changes. The approach combines an initial fetch with a subscription so the UI is always accurate. First, derive the PDA for the user's counter and perform an initial program. account. counter. fetch to set the counter value. Second, call connection. onAccountChange with the PDA and a callback that deserializes accountInfo. data using program. coder. accounts. decode, then call setCounterValue. Third, store the listener id and return a cleanup function that calls connection. removeAccountChangeListener(id). A concrete example is provided in the chapter and shows handling decode errors inside the callback; log and ignore decode problems so a transient update does not crash the UI. A common error is forgetting to guard for missing program or connection, producing runtime exceptions. Also avoid calling setState on an unmounted component by removing the listener in the cleanup. This pattern ensures the user sees immediate updates after any state change on-chain, and it prevents memory leaks or duplicated listeners when dependencies change. Implementing onAccountChange in useEffect means combine initial fetch with onaccountchange and remove the listener on unmount.. In practical terms, a step-by-step example for fullcounterdapp. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cleaning up listeners is essential to avoid memory leaks, duplicate callbacks, and confusing UI updates. When a component mounts it may add an onAccountChange listener; if the component unmounts or dependencies change without removing that listener, callbacks can continue to run and attempt to update state for an unmounted component. The process is straightforward: store the listener id returned by connection. onAccountChange, and in the useEffect cleanup call connection. removeAccountChangeListener(id) if id is not null. An example flow: start loading, compute PDA, fetch initial data, set up listener and save its id, and finally return a cleanup closure that removes the listener. A common misconception is that React will automatically remove external subscriptions; it won't. Another pitfall is not handling async setup order, which can cause the cleanup to have no id. To avoid this, declare the listener id in the outer scope of the effect and set it inside the async setup function. The practical benefit is predictable behavior: when the user navigates away or switches wallets, your app stops listening, preventing stale updates and console noise. Cleaning up listeners and avoiding memory leaks means store listener ids and remove them in the cleanup to prevent background callbacks and leaks.. In practical terms, why and how to remove account change listeners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transactions on Solana go through stages: you send a transaction and receive a signature, validators process it, and the network reaches a chosen confirmation level such as confirmed or finalized. For a great UX, your app should surface these stages to the user.
